entry.title: Sales Order Stock (E) in SAP Logistics Management
entry.content:
Introduction

In make-to-order (MTO) and purchase-to-order (PTO) scenarios, goods are procured or produced exclusively for a specific customer and must only be supplied to that customer. Sales Order Stock, identified by special stock type “Sales Order Stock (E)”, ensures exactly this: a quantity of a product is reserved for one sales order and item, never available for any other sales order.

We are pleased to announce that SAP Logistics Management now supports special stock type Sales Order Stock (E).

Inbound

When an inbound delivery with a sales order reference is replicated to SAP Logistics Management, the logistical demand item carries the special stock type “Sales Order Stock (E)” and the sales order reference. In the Manage Inbound Warehouse Activities app, the logistics clerk can see that an incoming inbound warehouse request is tied to a specific sales order.

Stock Management

After goods receipt, Sales Order Stock is fully visible in the Manage Stock app. The logistics clerk can filter by special stock type and view the sales order reference alongside other stock attributes. The sales order reference is hereby a quant separating attribute.

Warehouse Tasks

Warehouse tasks for putaway, picking, and internal movements now carry the special stock type and the sales order reference as part of the task data. can see on every task that the product belongs to a specific sales order.

 

Outbound

When an outbound delivery with sales order stock is transferred to SAP Logistics Management, the logistical demand item and the outbound warehouse request item show the special stock type Sales Order Stock (E) and the sales order reference. With that in place, the system ensures that the right stock – that is, stock with exactly the same sales order reference – will be determined during picking warehouse task creation.

 

Stock Reconciliation

The Reconcile Stock app in SAP Logistics Management also supports Sales Order Stock (E). The logistics clerk can filter by special stock type to view all Sales Order Stock, including the quantities held in SAP Logistics Management and SAP S/4HANA. Where discrepancies exist, the clerk can post the difference to SAP S/4HANA to bring both systems back into alignment.

 Conclusion

The introduction of support for Sales Order Stock (E) in SAP Logistics Management closes an important gap for customers running make-to-order scenarios and purchase-to-order scenarios.

This means manufacturers and distributors who work with sales order-specific inventory can execute their warehousing operations within SAP Logistics Management, with confidence that stock segregation is enforced at every step.

entry.title: Extensibility Options for Third-Party Payments
entry.content:
Introduction

Please note that the feature of this blog post is only for SAP S/4HANA Cloud Public Edition. 

When importing third-party payment files or return files via the Manage Incoming Payment Files app (F1680) the system parses the file and maps the raw data to internal structures using the Map Format data app. However, the default mapping may not always fit your specific business requirements.

Two Business Add-In (BAdI) extension points are delivered to adjust the mapped data at batch header and item level. Before the mapped data is written to the staging tables — you can change these values according to the business requirements.

The adjusted staging data is then consumed in the second step by the Process Imported Third-Party Payments app, which creates the actual Contract Accounting payment lots and return lots. Any changes you have made in the BAdI are therefore reflected in the final posted lot. This blog post introduces the procedure of importing and processing the external files. You can also learn about how to adjust the mapped data using the BadIs. For more information about the related blog posts, see the following links:

  • Payment Lot Data Import via Third-Party Payments - SAP Community
  • Return Lot File Import via Third- Party Payments - SAP Community

Where the Extension Point Runs

The diagram below shows the flow after you get the external files to the posting lots  in Contract Accounting:

  1. The external file is first uploaded via the Manage Incoming Payment Files app, where the Map Format Data for Third Party Payments app transform the bank/collector-specific (external) format into internal structures.
  2. After this mapping, the corresponding Badi is triggered, when you can adjust the data, before the data is written to the staging tables.
  3. Then you use the  Process Imported Third-Party Payments app to pick up the  staging data and create the final Payment Lot or Return Lot.

Business Add-Ins

  • BAdI for Payment Lot Import — BADI_FKKID_EXPC_PAYMENT_LOT

    This BAdI is called during the import of third-party payment files in Contract Accounting. It allows you to modify the mapped payment data before it is stored in the staging area; the adjusted data is subsequently used to create a Payment (Order) Lot in Contract Accounting.
  • BAdI for Return Lot Import — BADI_FKKID_EXPC_RETURN_LOT

    This BAdI is called during the import of third-party return files in Contract Accounting. It allows you to modify the mapped return data before it is stored in the staging area; the adjusted data is subsequently used to create a Return Lot in Contract Accounting.

Note:
The BAdI is called once per imported batch. It receives the complete lot header and the full table of items for that batch as changing parameters. This means you can modify any field on any existing item, but you cannot add or remove items and item numbers cannot be changed.

Implementation: Custom Logic App

As a key user, you can use the cloud business add-in (BAdI) to implement your own logic. Before using the cloud BAdI, ensure that you have assigned the business role SAP_BR_EXTENSIBILITY_SPEC.

Note: Regarding of extensibility options for developers, go to Business Accelerator Hub and search for Adjust Payment Data (for Customer).

  1. Open Custom Logic app. Select “Create”.
  2.  In the search box, search for the BAdI name:
    1. For Payment Lot: BADI_FKKID_EXPC_PAYMENT_LOT
    2. For Return Lot: BADI_FKKID_EXPC_RETURN_LOT and search.
  3. The extension point appears in the list with its description. Select it using the radio button, then click Step 2.
  4. Click Add to add a filter row. Select “Add” in the pop-up window to apply filter condition.
  5. Set the connector THIRDPARTYPAYMENTFORMATTYPE equal to your format type value:
    1. For Payment Lot:  THIRDPARTYPAYMENTFORMATTYPE = FICA-PAYMENT-LOT
    2. For Return Lot: THIRDPARTYPAYMENTFORMATTYPE = FICA-RETURN-LOT. Save the entries.
  6. After you save the condition, the filter with the format is visible. This ensures the BAdI is only triggered for files of the matching format type. Click Step3.
  7. Provide a meaningful description and a unique implementation ID (Create an implementation ID  starting with YY1_):
  8. Click Review and Create.
  9. Select Publish. You can then Open Code Editor.
  10. You can select Show Sample Code and copy them to clipboard to better change the coding based on your business needs.
  11. Click Edit and write your implement the logic based on your business requirements, then  select Save and Publish.

The implementation takes effect immediately on the next file import. It is not required to restart the system or transport.

Monitoring the Changes with Cloud BadIs

  • Upload the files after the Cloud BAdI Implementation

    1. Open the Manage Incoming Payment Files (F1680) app.
    2. Select Import and choose Third-party Payment to upload the files
    3. Select Payment Lot Data (Contract Accounting) as format.
    4. Upload the file and process.

  • View the changes in the Monitor Third-Party Payment app

    1. Open the Monitor Third-Party Payment app.
    2. Select row with imported file and here are results that are marked in yellow.

Is this blog post useful to you? Leave your comments below to let us know your thoughts.

entry.title: Re: BADI or API to make Material short text description a...
entry.content:
@RaymondGiuseppi you are right, and my accepted answer is wrong for a standard field. Thanks for catching it. I'm posting the correction as a new answer because it needs code, and the comment box doesn't take it.

I went back to the code in an S/4HANA 2023 system. FIELDSELECTION_ITEM of ME_PROCESS_REQ_CUST is called from function module MEREQBADI_FS_ITEM, and before the call it copies only the rows with metafield >= MMMFD_CUST_01, which is 90000000. The comment in the code even says "firewall". The short text is MMMFD_SHORT_TEXT, value 069, so it never reaches the BAdI and the READ TABLE in my example simply finds nothing. The same function in a 2020 system has the same filter.

What does reach the short text is in the same function, a few lines below: the BAdI MM_PUR_S4_PR_FLDCNTRL_SIMPLE (interface IF_MM_PUR_S4_PR_FLDCNTRL, method MODIFY_FIELDCONTROLS). It gets the standard fields with a global field name, the short text is mapped as PURCHASEREQUISITIONITEMTEXT (metafield 69), and the status you return is written back to the metafield after the call.

So for the original question, this is the version I should have posted:

METHOD if_mm_pur_s4_pr_fldcntrl~modify_fieldcontrols.
  " only items with a material: a free-text item still needs the field
  IF purchaserequisitionitem-material IS INITIAL.
    RETURN.
  ENDIF.
  LOOP AT fieldselection_table ASSIGNING FIELD-SYMBOL(<ls_field>)
       WHERE field = 'PURCHASEREQUISITIONITEMTEXT'.
    <ls_field>-fieldstatus = '*'.   " display only
  ENDLOOP.
ENDMETHOD.

The values are the same as before ('*' display, '-' hidden, '+' required, '.' optional, from IF_MMPUR_CONSTANTS_STATUS). The enhancement spot is released for key user apps in 2020 and 2023, so it can be implemented in the Custom Logic app, and in 2023 it is also released for ABAP Cloud.

What I checked: the method compiles against the BAdI interface in S/4HANA 2023 (syntax check only, nothing saved), and the same code with a wrong component name fails. I didn't run ME51N with it, and I didn't check the Fiori apps or Public Cloud.

entry.title: SAP Business Network for Logistics – Carrier API Integration for Real-Time Shipment Tracking
entry.content:
Introduction

SAP Business Network for Logistics (SAP BN4L) enables seamless digital collaboration between shippers, carriers, and logistics partners across the end-to-end freight lifecycle. Through the Global Track and Trace (GTT) capability, shippers gain real-time visibility into shipment execution — and carriers can provide that visibility directly via API.

While the companion blog post SAP Business Network for Logistics – Carrier API Integration for Road Subcontracting covers how freight orders are awarded and confirmed, this post focuses on the tracking integration from the carrier's perspective: how to receive tracking requests and how to report shipment events back to the shipper in real time.

Note: The examples in this post focus on road freight (FTL / full-truck-load). SAP BN4L also supports ocean, air, and parcel freight — the event model differs for those modes.

 

Summary

This blog post covers the end-to-end carrier-side implementation of real-time shipment tracking via the APIs provided by SAP Business Network for Logistics.

 

Prerequisites

Before implementing the subcontracting API integration, ensure the following:

  • You have access to a SAP BN4L carrier portal (test or productive). If you don’t have access to a SAP BN4L carrier tenant yet, ask your shipper to invite you to join the network using the Invite Business Partners app. Once invited, you’ll receive an e-mail notification with registration link. After registration, you’ll have access to the SAP BN4L carrier portal.
  • Get familiar with basic carrier onboarding steps (see blog: "Getting Started with Carrier API Integration in 3 Simple Steps")
  • Start getting familiar with the inbound/outbound SAP BN4L APIs for tracking on the SAP Business Accelerator Hub: Consumer API for Tracking and Provider API for Tracking
  • You have a webhook endpoint ready to receive HTTP PUT and DELETE requests from SAP BN4L.

 

Understanding the Tracking Message Flow

Tracking is a two-phase integration. First, the shipper activates tracking on a freight order, which triggers the inbound flow to your webhook endpoint. From there, your system continuously reports events outbound to SAP BN4L until tracking is deactivated.

For the tracking request from shippers to your webhook endpoint, the SAP BN4L Consumer API for Tracking structure is used.

For the tracking information shared by the carrier/Visibility Provider, SAP BN4L provides the Provider API for Tracking

The full API structure is specified in the links above on the SAP Business Accelerator Hub.

 

Step 1: Register Webhook Endpoints in SAP BN4L

The first step is to configure your carrier tenant so that SAP BN4L knows where to route tracking messages. This is done in the System Connections app.

Your webhook endpoint must support the following three operations:

OperationHTTP MethodUse Case
Put order for trackingPUTReceive creation or updates to an existing tracking request (e.g., stop changes)
Delete order for TrackingDELETEReceive tracking deactivation — stop reporting events after this

 

Use the Connection Wizard

In your SAP BN4L carrier tenant, navigate to the System Connections app and use the Connection Wizard to register your webhook endpoint following Scenario 1: Outbound API Connection described in the Simplify Your Integration Setup with the Connection Wizard in System Connections blogpost. Repeat for all two operations above. You may use the same webhook base URL for all three if your endpoint supports all operations.

 

Note: Inside the wizard in step 4 (Communication), provide the base URL of your webhook with /LBNOrderForTracking/.

When SAP BN4L routes a tracking request to your webhook, it authenticates using the credentials you configure during the Connection Wizard setup. The supported authentication scheme is Basic Authentication, OAuth 2.0 and API Key. When calling your webhook endpoints SAP BN4L sends these credentials with every outbound HTTP request. Make sure your webhook validates incoming requests against these credentials to ensure only SAP BN4L can push messages to your system.

The credentials you configure in the connection wizard need to be shared with the shipper so they can configure the connection to your endpoints on their side and authenticate against your webhook endpoint when SAP BN4L routes messages to you.

 

Required Connections

To fully enable API based creation, update and cancellation of freight orders to your webhook, your Outbound Connections should look as follows. Make sure all connections are in status Active.

 

Step 2: Process Tracking Request

When the shipper activates tracking on a freight order, SAP BN4L sends a tracking request (HTTP PUT) to your webhook endpoint. This payload is the foundation of your entire tracking integration.

Note: When receiving a tracking request, the http reponse should contain a parameter trackid  with a value as payload body. Ideally, this should contain the tracking ID which the carrier uses as transport reference. In case of  asynchronous processing, a dummy value can be used.

 

Mandatory identifiers to be stored

 The following fields are at least to be stored on carrier side as they will be needed for event reporting:

  • shipper.shipperLBNID representing the network identifier of the shipper within the SAP BN4L network
  • carrier.carrierLBNID  representing the network identifier of the carrier within the SAP BN4L network
  • technicalId representing the unique process identifier of the tracked process within SAP BN4L
  • stops along with stopId and locationId
  • orderId reflects the freight order ID which was already shared during subcontracting

 

The technicalId — Your Most Important Field

The technicalId is a structured string that uniquely identifies the tracked shipment within SAP BN4L. Every event you report must include exactly this value. Any mismatch results in a silent processing failure.

Segment

Example Value

Meaning

Prefix

xri://sap.com/id

SAP XRI identifier prefix

Shipper LBN ID

LBN#10020009999

The shipper's LBN ID

Originator

S4HCLNT001

The shipper's system identifier

Object Type

FT1_SHIPMENT

The tracked object type

Freight Order ID

6100010556

The freight order ID from the shipper's system

Suffix

GTT

GTT = shipper operates a dedicated SAP GTT tenant.

 Note: Example technicalId: xri://sap.com/id:LBN#10020009999:S4HCLNT001:FT1_SHIPMENT:6100010556:GTT
Store and replay this value exactly as received. Any mismatch will cause your events to fail silently during async processing.

Make sure to also be able to handle tracking request updates in accordance to step 1 when you enabled the put operation.

When looking for a list of possibly occuring values of reason codes, event codes, modes of transport, tracked object types etc. Check the following link: Code Lists 

 

Carrier Reference Document and Shipper Reference Documents

When subcontracting takes place outside of BN4L, the carrier typically has no knowledge of the shipper's internal freight order number. If a shared transport identifier was established during the subcontracting process, it can easily be included in the tracking request through the carrierReferenceDocuments or shipperReferenceDocuments array — serving as a reliable bridge between the systems of both parties.

 

Understanding the Stops Array

The stops[] array defines the planned stops the shipper expects to track — loading, unloading, and any intermediate stops — along with the planned event types expected at each. Use only the event types present in stops[].plannedEvents — do not hardcode a fixed list. Anything beyond those defined in the tracking request is treated as an unplanned event.

Each stop is always associated with a location — either as a structured address or a geo-coordinate. Carrier systems can therefore derive location information directly from the stops array, which is also relevant when reporting milestones: if the shipper uses location matching to correlate incoming events to planned events, the location data embedded in the stops provides the reference information for that matching.

Below is a minimal example of the inbound tracking request payload, showing the stops structure:

 

"stops": [
    {
      "stopId": "61000105560001",
      "ordinalNo": 1,
      "location": {
        "Id": "xri://sap.com/id:LBN#10020009999:CLNT100:Location:LogisticLocation:SP_0041",
        "address": {
          "city": "Shipstadt",
          […],
          "street": "SHIPPER-Weg"
        },
        "timeZone": "CET",
        "latitude": 49.2933,
        "longitude": 8.6431,
        "splcCode": ""
      },
      "plannedEvents": [
        […],
        {
          "eventType": "DEPARTURE",
          […],
          "plannedBusinessTimestamp": "2025-12-18T09:26:46Z",
          "eventMatchKey": "61000105560001"
        }
      ]
    },
    {
      "stopId": "61000105560002",
      "ordinalNo": 2,
      "location": {
        "Id": "xri://sap.com/id:LBN#10020009999:CLNT100:Location:LogisticLocation:0000410003",
        "address": {
          "city": "Linz",
          "country": "AT",
          […],
          "street": "Customerweg"
        },
        "timeZone": "CET",
        "latitude": 48.4431,
        "longitude": 14.59163,
        "splcCode": ""
      },
      "plannedEvents": [
        {
          "eventType": "ARRIV_DEST",
          […],
          "plannedBusinessTimestamp": "2025-12-21T23:00:00Z",
          "eventMatchKey": "61000105560002"
        },
        […],
        {
          "eventType": "POD",
          […],
          "plannedBusinessTimestamp": "2025-12-21T23:00:00Z",
          "eventMatchKey": "61000105560002"
        }
      ]
    }
  ]

Note: The event types listed in stops[].plannedEvents are defined by the shipper's GTT model configuration. Always derive your list of valid planned event types from the tracking request — never assume a fixed set.

 

Step 3: Test Your Webhook

Once the webhooks are registered, you can test the connection directly in the System Connections app using the Test Service button. You can either test with a default payload provided by SAP or request a custom payload from your shipper.

The Test Service functionality can be executed for all services/endpoints (create/update/cancel) by selecting a line in the Service table and using the Test Service button. This functionality will trigger the payloads directly to your registered webhooks.

 

Step 4: Report Tracking Events

As the shipment moves, your system sends events to SAP BN4L via the GTT Order Events Provider API. Events fall into two categories: planned milestones (tied to a known stop) and unplanned events (not tied to a specific stop).

Use the following endpoint to send your subcontracting confirmation/rejection to the shipper:

POST https://api.logistics.eu.business-network.cloud.sap/http/http/v1/tracking/events/OrderEvents

Requests to SAP BN4L must be authenticated via OAuth 2.0. You can retrieve authentication details from the System Connections app via Connection Settings > Show Service Credentials as long as Enable Inbound Connections is enabled:

The following table explains the structure of every event (except for ETA updates) and how the fields should be populated:

API Field

Description/Value

Mapped field in Tracking Request API

Mandatory

shipper.shipperLBNID

ID of the shipper in the BNL network (different in dev/prod)

shipper.shipperLBNID

Yes

carrier.carrierLBNID

ID of the carrier in the BNL network (different in dev/prod)

carrier.carrierLBNID

Yes

creationDateTimeUTC

Timestamp of event creation/trigger to GTT in UTC format: yyyy-mm-ddThh:mm:ssZ

 

Yes

technicalId

Unique process identifier

technicalId

Yes

events.natureOfEvent

“01” or “02”

 

Yes

events.eventType

e.g.

“DEPARTURE” 🡪 Departure,

“ARRIV_DEST” 🡪 Arrival,

“EVENT_EST_UPD” 🡪 ETA Update

 

Yes

events.stopId

Reflects either the stop ID of the loading location or the unloading location

shipment.stops.stopId

Yes

events.location.Id

Reflects the unique location ID of the loading or unloading location

shipment.stops.location.Id

No

events.eventDateTimeUTC

Actual Timestamp when the event occurred in UTC format: yyyy-mm-ddThh:mm:ssZ

 

Yes

 For GPS updates (event type GEOLOC) GPS positions are expected to be provided as well:

  • events.location.latitude
  • events.location.longitude

 

Planned Milestones — Provide stopId

These are expected at specific stops as defined in stops[].plannedEvents of the tracking request (i.e., the planned event types / planned milestones). Provide the stopId from the tracking request — SAP BN4L already knows the location.

Event Type

Description

ARRIV_DEST

Arrival at location

DEPARTURE

Departure from a stop

LOAD_BEGIN

Loading start

LOAD_END

Loading end

ARRIV_DEST

Arrival at destination

UNLOAD_BEGIN

Unloading start

UNLOAD_END

Unloading end

POD

Proof of delivery

CHECK_IN

Check-in at location

 Note: The event types above are common examples. The authoritative list for your integration is defined by the shipper's GTT model — use only the event types present in the stops[].plannedEvents array of the tracking request.

For a complete list of availabel event codes, please refer to the following list: List of available event codes 

Unplanned Events — Provide Coordinates or Reason Codes

These are not tied to a planned stop. Provide location data or reason codes directly in the event payload.

Event Type

Description

GEOLOC

GPS position update — provide latitude and longitude

EVENT_EST_UPD

Estimated time update for any planned stop event — specify the target event type in estimatedEvent.eventType

DELAY

Delay notification with reason code

 Note: Best practice - Always pair a DELAY event with an EVENT_EST_UPD so the shipper sees both the cause of the delay and the updated expected arrival time.

Send ETAs proactively. Every time your system recalculates an arrival estimate, send EVENT_EST_UPD. Shippers use them for dock scheduling and customer commitments.

For a complete list of available reason codes, please refer to the following list: List of available reason codes 

Subsequently, you can find example payloads of common events for your reference.

Example: Departure from a Planned Stop

{
  "shipper": { "shipperLBNID": "10020009999" },
  "carrier": { "carrierLBNID": "10020003333" },
  "orderId": "6100010556",
  "technicalId": "xri://sap.com/id:LBN#10020009999:S4HCLNT001:FT1_SHIPMENT:6100010556:GTT",
  "events": [{
    "eventType": "DEPARTURE",
    "eventDateTimeUTC": "2026-07-15T08:35:00Z",
    "stopId": "61000105560001"
  }]
}

 

Example: GPS Position Update (Unplanned)

{
  "shipper": { "shipperLBNID": "10020009999" },
  "carrier": { "carrierLBNID": "10020003333" },
  "orderId": "6100010556",
  "technicalId": "xri://sap.com/id:LBN#10020009999:S4HCLNT001:FT1_SHIPMENT:6100010556:GTT",
  "events": [{
    "eventType": "GEOLOC",
    "eventDateTimeUTC": "2026-07-15T11:20:00Z",
    "longitude": 13.4176
    "latitude": 52.5497
  }]
}

 

Example: ETA Update (Unplanned)

{
  "shipper": { "shipperLBNID": "10020009999" },
  "carrier": { "carrierLBNID": "10020003333" },
  "orderId": "6100010556",

  "events": [{
    "eventType": "EVENT_EST_UPD",
    "creationDateTimeUTC": "2026-07-15T10:00:00Z",
    "estimatedEvent": {
      "eventType": "ARRIV_DEST",
      "stopId": "61000105560002",
      "estimatedDateTimeUTC": "2026-07-16T16:30:00Z"
    }
  }]
}
// creationDateTimeUTC = when your system calculated this estimate
// estimatedDateTimeUTC = the predicted arrival time
// stopid = referencing the stop where the arrival will take place

 

Example: Delay with Paired ETA Update (Best Practice)

{
  "shipper": { "shipperLBNID": "10020009999" },
  "carrier": { "carrierLBNID": "10020003333" },
  "orderId": "6100010556",
  "technicalId": "xri://sap.com/id:LBN#10020009999:S4HCLNT001:FT1_SHIPMENT:6100010556:GTT",
  "events": [
    {
      "eventType": "DELAY",
      "eventDateTimeUTC": "2026-07-15T14:00:00Z",
      "delayReasonCode": "TRAFFIC"
    },
    {
      "eventType": "EVENT_EST_UPD",
      "creationDateTimeUTC": "2026-07-15T14:00:00Z",
      "estimatedEvent": {
        "eventType": "ARRIV_DEST",
        "stopId": "61000105560002",
        "estimatedDateTimeUTC": "2026-07-16T18:00:00Z"
      }
    }
  ]
}

 

Sending Multiple Events in One Request

The events[] array accepts multiple entries per API call. When several milestones occur at the same stop at roughly the same time, submit them in a single request:

{
  "shipper": { "shipperLBNID": "10020009999" },
  "carrier": { "carrierLBNID": "10020003333" },
  "orderId": "6100010556",
  "technicalId": "xri://sap.com/id:LBN#10020009999:S4HCLNT001:FT1_SHIPMENT:6100010556:GTT",
  "events": [
    { "eventType": "UNLOAD_END", "eventDateTimeUTC": "2026-07-16T15:45:00Z", "stopId": "61000105560002" },
    { "eventType": "POD",        "eventDateTimeUTC": "2026-07-16T15:50:00Z", "stopId": "61000105560002" }
  ]
}

 

Step 5: Handle Tracking Deactivation and Order Cancellation

Your webhook endpoint will receive messages that end the tracking lifecycle. Your integration must handle two distinct scenarios:

 

Tracking Deactivation (HTTP DELETE)

The shipper explicitly deactivates tracking — for example, because the carrier assignment changed or tracking is no longer needed. When you receive this message, stop sending events for the corresponding technicalId immediately.

{
  "shipper": { "shipperLBNID": "10020009999" },
  "carrier": { "carrierLBNID": "10020003333" },
  "orderId": "6100010556",
  "technicalId": "xri://sap.com/id:LBN#10020009999:S4HCLNT001:FT1_SHIPMENT:6100010556:GTT"
}

Note: Continuing to submit events after deactivation results in SILENT processing failures with no error feedback.

 

Order Cancellation

If the shipper cancels the freight order entirely, SAP BN4L routes a cancellation notification to your webhook endpoint. Mark the order as cancelled and suppress all future event submissions for that order.

 

Step 6: Monitor the Integration

SAP BN4L provides the Manage Integration Logs app in your carrier tenant, which records all inbound and outbound message exchanges. Use this app to verify whether tracking requests were successfully delivered to your webhook, inspect payload details, and troubleshoot failed or missing messages. During initial development and testing, this is your primary tool for debugging integration issues. It is also useful in productive scenarios to trace message flow when discrepancies arise between your system and the shipper's freight order data.

Note: An HTTP 200 response from the GTT Order Events Provider API confirms RECEIPT, not successful semantic processing. Use the Manage Integration Logs app to verify whether events were actually processed — semantic errors (wrong field values, mismatched technicalId) are silently dropped.

 

Practical Integration Tips

Tip

Guidance

Store the full tracking request

Store the technicalId, all planned stopId values, and the planned event types per stop. Keep the full payload for audit and replay purposes.

Let the request define what's planned

Do NOT hardcode event types. Read them from stops[].plannedEvents — anything beyond those is an unplanned event.

Use UTC everywhere

All timestamps — eventDateTimeUTC, creationDateTimeUTC, estimatedDateTimeUTC — must be UTC.

Report actual event timestamps

Always set eventDateTimeUTC to the actual time of the event, even if you submit it with delay. GTT uses this field to order events — do not use the submission time.

Send ETAs proactively

Every time your system recalculates an arrival estimate, send EVENT_EST_UPD. Pair every DELAY with an ETA update.

Batch co-occurring events

When multiple milestones happen at the same stop at the same time, send them in a single API call using events[].

Retry safely

SAP BN4L deduplicates events with the same technicalId, eventType, stopId, and eventDateTimeUTC. Safe to retry on transient HTTP 5xx errors — do not change the payload on retry.

Include your shipment reference

Use the optional carrierOrderId field in event payloads to include your internal reference for cross-system traceability.

Test end-to-end before go-live

Semantic errors are silently dropped. Use Manage Integration Logs during development. End-to-end testing in a non-productive environment is the only safe validation approach.

 If you are also interested in setting up the API integration of the subcontracting flow, you can find more information here: 

SAP Business Network for Logistics – Carrier API Integration for Road Subcontracting 

 

Conclusion

Implementing real-time shipment tracking via the SAP Business Network for Logistics APIs follows a clear pattern once you understand the message flow: register your webhook endpoints, store the tracking request with all its identifiers, report events as they occur, and stop when deactivation arrives.

The two fields that matter most throughout are technicalId and stopId. Get those right and the integration works reliably. Get them wrong and events are silently dropped — with no error response to tell you why. This is why end-to-end testing in a non-productive environment using the Manage Integration Logs app is highly recommended; it is the only way to confirm that events are semantically processed, not just received.

A few principles carry the most weight in practice:

  •   Let the tracking request define the transport from the shipper's point of view. Read planned event types from stops[].plannedEvents. Do not hardcode them.
  •   Replay the technicalId exactly. Copy it character-for-character from the inbound payload. Never construct it yourself.
  •   Send ETAs proactively. Pair every DELAY with an EVENT_EST_UPD. Shippers use these for dock scheduling and customer commitments.
  •   Handle deactivation immediately. Once an HTTP DELETE arrives, stop submitting events for that technicalId. Continued submissions fail silently.

With these foundations in place, your system becomes a reliable visibility source for the shipper — enabling the real-time freight transparency that SAP BN4L is designed to deliver.

entry.title: SAP Business Network for Logistics – Carrier API Integration for Road Subcontracting
entry.content:
Introduction

SAP Business Network for Logistics (BN4L) enables seamless digital collaboration between shippers, carriers, and logistics partners across the end-to-end freight lifecycle. Through the Freight Collaboration capability, shippers can send subcontracting requests (freight orders) to carriers via standardized REST APIs, replacing manual communication channels such as email or phone.

While previous blog posts in this context have covered how to get started with carrier API integration and the ocean freight booking APIs, this post focuses specifically on the subcontracting flow for road freight orders from carrier’s perspective. We will walk through the complete lifecycle: receiving a subcontracting request, handling updates and cancellations, and sending a confirmation or rejection back to the shipper.

Note: With 2608 release, a new connection wizard was introduced initial steps on carrier side. The new functionality is described in blog post Simplify Your Integration Setup with the Connection Wizard in System Connections.

Note: If tracking freight orders is also in scope through BN4L, please refer to the companion blog post SAP Business Network for Logistics – Carrier API Integration for Real-Time Shipment Tracking for further details.

 

Summary

This blog post covers the end-to-end carrier-side implementation of road freight subcontracting via the APIs provided by SAP Business Network for Logistics.

The key steps are:

 

Prerequisites

Before implementing the subcontracting API integration, ensure the following:

  • You have access to a BN4L carrier portal (test or productive). If you don’t have access to a BN4L carrier tenant yet, ask your shipper to invite you to join the network using the Invite Business Partners app. Once invited, you’ll receive an e-mail notification with registration link. After registration, you’ll have access to the BN4L carrier portal.
  • Get familiar with basic carrier onboarding steps (see blog: "Getting Started with Carrier API Integration in 3 Simple Steps")
  • Start getting familiar with the inbound/outbound SAP BN4L APIs for subcontracting on the SAP Business Accelerator Hub: Consumer API for Freight Subcontracting and Provider API for Freight Subcontracting
  • You have a webhook endpoint ready to receive HTTP POST and PUT requests from BN4L.

 

Understanding the Subcontracting Message Flow

The subcontracting process in BN4L follows two integration flows:

For the subcontracting request from shippers to your webhook endpoint, the SAP BN4L Consumer API for Freight Subcontracting structure is used.

For the subcontracting response (confirmation/rejection), SAP BN4L provides the Provider API for Freight Subcontracting.

The full API structure is specified in the links above on the SAP Business Accelerator Hub.

 

Step 1: Register Webhook Endpoints in BN4L

The first step is to configure your carrier tenant so that BN4L knows where to route subcontracting messages from the shipper. This is done in the System Connections app.

To handle the full subcontracting lifecycle, your webhook must support the following relative paths:

Relative Endpoint Path

Use Case

HTTP Method

Comments

/LbnFreightOrderFor
Subcontracting

Initial subcontracting
request (new freight order)

POST

Shipper creates a new freight order and sends it to the carrier

/LbnFreightOrderFor
Subcontracting
/{orderingPartyLbnId}
/{originatorId}
/{freightOrderId}

Update to existing
freight order

PUT

Identifiers are passed as URL
path parameters (not in the body)

/LbnFreightOrderFor
Subcontracting
/{orderingPartyLbnId}
/{originatorId}
/{freightOrderId}
/cancellation

Cancel existing
freight order

POST

Triggered when shipper cancels
a previously sent freight order

 

Use the Connection Wizard

In your BN4L carrier tenant, navigate to the System Connections app and use the Connection Wizard to register your webhook endpoint for subcontracting following “Scenario 1: Outbound API Connection” described in the Simplify Your Integration Setup with the Connection Wizard in System Connections blogpost.

 

Manage Webhooks

To enable all relevant subcontracting flows, you need to repeat the steps in the Connection Wizard to enable the following 3 operations. You can use the same webhook endpoint and credentials if your endpoint supports all 3 operations also described in above table.

Inside the wizard in step 4 (Communication), provide the base URL of your webhook without BN4L specific suffix /LbnFreightOrderForSubcontracting documented in the beginning of this chapter. This suffix will automatically be added when BN4L calls your webhook.

When BN4L routes a subcontracting request to your webhook, it authenticates using the credentials you configure during the Connection Wizard setup. The supported authentication scheme is Basic Authentication, OAuth 2.0 and API Key. When calling your webhook endpoints BN4L sends these credentials with every outbound HTTP request. Make sure your webhook validates incoming requests against these credentials to ensure only BN4L can push messages to your system.

The credentials you configure in the connection wizard need to be shared with the shipper so they can configure the connection to your endpoints on their side and authenticate against your webhook endpoint when BN4L routes messages to you.

 

Required Connections

To fully enable API-based creation, update and cancellation of freight orders to your webhook, your Outbound Connections should look as follows. Make sure all connections are in status Active.

 

 

Step 2: Process Subcontracting Request

When you receive the initial subcontracting request (HTTP POST) to your webhook endpoint, certain fields are critical and must be stored on your side. These identifiers are included in the initial payload but are not repeated in subsequent update messages – instead, they become part of the URL path parameters in succeeding HTTP PUT requests.

Closely collaborate with your shipper to align completeness of required information to subcontract a freight order. In case any information in the API structure is missing but mandatory, ask your shipper to transfer missing information in the notes segment with dedicated note types to easily identify missing information.

Check the API documentation for the Consumer API for Freight Subcontracting for the full API structure documentation.

For example payloads, refer to the appendix at the bottom of this blog post or use the Test Service functionality described in Step 4: Test Your Webhook.

 

Linking Items to Loading/Unloading Locations

Items with their packages and quantities are linked to loading and unloading locations via the transportationStages array. Each transportation stage contains an assignedItems array that references freight order items by their items.id. This linkage is essential if you need to determine which items are picked up or delivered at which location.

 

Handling Codes in the Subcontracting Payload

SAP Business Network for Logistics maintains a standardized set of code values for the various business attributes used across the platform transmitted in the subcontracting request payload. These codes are exchanged as part of B2B communication and integration processes to ensure that business information is interpreted consistently by all participating parties, such as shippers and carriers.

The definition of the codes used in the payload is documented and maintained on the SAP Help Portal:
https://help.sap.com/docs/business-network-freight-collaboration/code-lists/code-lists 

In addition to the standard BN4L code values, shippers may choose to use their own custom codes. In such cases, the corresponding code mappings and business semantics must be agreed upon and aligned between the shipper and carrier as part of the integration project to ensure seamless data exchange and correct interpretation of the transmitted information.

 

Step 3: Handling Freight Order Updates

After the initial subcontracting request, the shipper may send updates via HTTP PUT to your webhook. Your system must be prepared to handle the following update cases:

Note: In update payloads (HTTP PUT), the freightOrderId, originatorId, and orderingPartyLbnId are passed as URL path parameters, not in the request body. This is why storing them from the initial POST is essential.

 

Step 4: Test Your Webhook

Once the webhooks are registered, you can test the connection directly in the System Connections app using the Test Service button. You can either test with a default payload provided by SAP or request a custom payload from your shipper.

The Test Service functionality can be executed for all services/endpoints (create/update/cancel) by selecting a line in the Service table and using the Test Service button. This functionality will trigger the payloads directly to your registered webhooks.

 

Step 5: Sending a Confirmation or Rejection

After receiving a subcontracting request, the carrier must respond with either a confirmation or a rejection. This is done by calling the BN4L Provider API for Freight Subcontracting via HTTP POST.

Subcontracting Confirmation API Endpoint

Use the following endpoint to send your subcontracting confirmation/rejection to the shipper:

POST https://api.logistics.eu.business-network.cloud.sap
     /http/v1/LbnFreightOrderForSubcontracting
     /{orderingPartyLbnId}/{originatorId}/{freightOrderId}/carrierResponse

Important: Replace the placeholders orderingPartyLbnId, originatorId and freightOrderId with the values received in the initial subcontracting request.

Requests to SAP BN4L must be authenticated via OAuth 2.0. You can retrieve authentication details from the System Connections app via Connection Settings > Show Service Credentials as long as Enable Inbound Connections is enabled:

Updating a Previously Sent Confirmation

After sending an initial confirmation, you may need to update the response — for example, to correct a license plate number, assign a different trailer, or add a note. The Provider API for Freight Subcontracting supports this by allowing you to send another HTTP POST to the same carrierResponse endpoint with the updated payload. BN4L will overwrite the previous response and forward the updated information to the shipper's transportation system. Make sure to always include all mandatory fields (carrierPartyLbnId, confirmationStatus) in the updated payload, not just the changed fields.

 

Step 6: Monitor the Integration

BN4L provides the Manage Integration Logs app in your carrier tenant, which records all inbound and outbound message exchanges. Use this app to verify whether subcontracting requests were successfully delivered to your webhook, inspect payload details, and troubleshoot failed or missing messages. During initial development and testing, this is your primary tool for debugging integration issues. It is also useful in productive scenarios to trace message flow when discrepancies arise between your system and the shipper's freight order data.

 

Conclusion

With the steps covered in this post, you now have a solid foundation to implement the full carrier-side subcontracting flow via SAP Business Network for Logistics:

  • Registering your webhook endpoints and configuring the required outbound connections
  • Processing incoming freight orders and correctly storing the identifiers needed for subsequent updates
  • Handling updates and cancellations without losing track of the freight order lifecycle
  • Responding to the shipper with a confirmation or rejection via the Provider API
  • Monitoring your integration using the Manage Integration Logs app

If tracking freight orders is also in scope through BN4L, please refer to the companion blog post SAP Business Network for Logistics – Carrier API Integration for Real-Time Shipment Tracking for further details on tracking via SAP BN4L.

My key takeaway from working with this integration: invest time upfront in aligning with your shipper on which fields are mandatory in your specific scenario. The API is flexible, but business agreements around missing data (especially around items, packaging, and time windows) will save you significant back-and-forth during testing.

If you're just getting started, the Test Service functionality in System Connections is your best friend — use it early and often during implementation.

Have questions or feedback? Drop them in the comments below. Whether you're stuck on a specific step or have suggestions to improve this guide — I'd love to hear from you. Your input helps make this resource better for the whole community.

entry.title: Re: SAP HANA access through MCP: recommended architecture...
entry.content:
Hi,

I build tooling and agents that talk to SAP systems, and I went through the same questions. For a HANA that sits under S/4HANA, the biggest problem with direct SQL is not even support or license. It is that the database gives you a different answer than the application.

I counted the same tables twice in my S/4HANA 2023 lab, once with ABAP SQL on the application server and once with native SQL on HANA, same client:

  • MSEG: 1,440 rows with ABAP SQL, 1 row with native SQL
  • MKPF: 1,020 and 1
  • ANEK: 20 and 0
  • MATDOC: 1,460 in both

The reason is the replacement object (field VIEWREF in DD02L). When ABAP reads MSEG, it is redirected to the CDS view NSDM_DDL_MSEG ("MSEG Compatibility View"), which reads MATDOC. Native SQL reads the old physical table, which is almost empty. In that lab 292 tables have a replacement object, 293 in my 2020 lab. An agent that writes SELECT ... FROM MSEG against HANA gets a confident wrong answer, and nothing tells it that.

On authorizations, your suspicion is right. CDS access controls (DCL) are applied by ABAP SQL, not by the database. The same 2023 lab has 44,460 access control objects. A database user with SELECT on the schema sees all company codes and sales orgs, because HANA privileges don't know about them, and the client (MANDT) is also your job in native SQL. Read-only removes the risk of breaking data, but not the wrong answer, the authorization gap, or the load of a heavy generated join on a productive system.

What I would do for S/4HANA: MCP server, then the application layer, never the database. Released OData APIs or released CDS views, called with the user's own identity (principal propagation), not with a technical user. Small tools with fixed queries and a row limit on the server side, instead of SQL written by the model. If you need flexible queries, run them as ABAP SQL on released CDS views, so the replacement objects, DCL and client handling still apply. There is a good SAP example of this pattern here in the Community, with principal propagation to S/4HANA: Joule A2A: MCP Gateway to S/4HANA with Principal Propagation.

A standalone HANA with your own schema is a different story: the data model is yours and HANA roles and analytic privileges are the authorization layer. For HANA Cloud, the SAP Architecture Center documents a local MCP server that ships with hana-ai, the Generative AI Toolkit for HANA Cloud, with audit of every tool call: HANA AI Toolkit Local MCP Server. I didn't find an official SAP MCP server for HANA under S/4HANA.

About license: if the HANA came with S/4HANA under a runtime license, access from your own application is usually not covered. I'm not a licensing person, so check that with your SAP account team before building on it.

What I measured: the counts above in S/4HANA 2023 (release 758) and the number of replacement objects and access controls in 2023 and 2020. I didn't test HANA Cloud or the hana-ai server.

entry.title: Handling Job Approval Rejection in SAP SmartRecruiters: Re-triggering Approvals via API
entry.content:
When Does SmartRecruiters Re-trigger Approval Automatically?

Before building an integration, it is important to understand the native behaviour. A re-approval is triggered automatically when any of the following position fields are updated:

  • Position Open Date
  • Target Start Date
  • Position Type
  • Position ID
  • Salary Range (min, max, currency)
Key Limitation: If an approver rejects the job asking for a change to a field not in the list above — such as job location, job advertisement text, or a custom job field — the system will not automatically re-trigger the approval after the update. An API-based integration is required.

The Integration Approach

The solution consists of four steps, all orchestrated by listening to a single webhook event fired by SmartRecruiters:

 

 

  Step 1    Detect the Rejection via Webhook

Configure the job.approval.step.rejected webhook event in SmartRecruiters. This event fires the moment any approval step is rejected, delivering the jobId and approval context to your integration endpoint.

 

Step 2    Retrieve the Approval ID

Use the job's ID (received from the webhook payload) to fetch the latest approval record. This call returns the approvalRequestId which is required for all further operations on that approval.

GET    https://api.smartrecruiters.com/jobs/{jobId}/approvals/latest

Example call:

https://api.smartrecruiters.com/jobs/33b57035-317d-4b4a-aa30-44d2e8cc928f/approvals/latest

 

 

  Step 3    Read the Rejection Reason (Optional but Recommended)

Before creating a new approval, fetch the approver's rejection comment. This allows your integration to log the reason, notify the recruiter, or route the notification differently based on the rejection message.

  GET    https://api.smartrecruiters.com/approvals-api/v201910/approvals/{approvalId}/comments

Example call:

https://api.smartrecruiters.com/approvals-api/v201910/approvals/801e28f7-e212-4859-9908-2935d0d25b37/comments

  Step 4    Create a New Approval

After the recruiter has made the requested changes, trigger a fresh approval by posting to the Approvals API. The key field is baseId — set it to the approvalRequestId retrieved in Step 2. This links the new approval to the original job context.

  POST    https://api.smartrecruiters.com/approvals-api/v201910/approvals

Request body:

{
  "baseId": "801e28f7-e212-4859-9908-2935d0d25b37",
  "type": "sequential",
  "decisionMode": "any",
  "steps": [
    {
      "approvers": [
        { "id": "6a986436be2958fa852dda78" }
      ]
    },
    {
      "approvers": [
        { "id": "6a98643697a14f8c43c2a454" }
      ]
    }
  ]
}

Response (201 Created):

"id": "f96a769b-788a-4fab-b1b3-bc9bacefba76",
    "subject": {
        "id": "33b57035-317d-4b4a-aa30-44d2e8cc928f",
        "type": "job"
    },
    "status": "PENDING",
    "type": "sequential",
    "decisionMode": "any",
    "steps": [
        {
            "status": "PENDING",
            "approvers": [
                {
                    "id": "6a986436be2958fa852dda78",
                    "decision": "PENDING"
                }
            ]
        },
        {
            "status": "PENDING",
            "approvers": [
                {
                    "id": "6a98643697a14f8c43c2a454",
                    "decision": "PENDING"
                }
            ]
        }
    ]
}

  • baseId: The approvalRequestId of the original (rejected) approval. Mandatory for re-approval.
  • type: sequential — approvers are notified one after another in order.
  • decisionMode: any — approval is granted once any approver in a step approves.
  • steps: An ordered array of approval steps, each containing one or more approver user IDs.

Verifying the Result in SmartRecruiters UI

After the API call succeeds, the job transitions through two visible states in the SmartRecruiters interface:

Before — Approval Rejected

 


 

After — New Approval Pending

 

Summary

When a job approval is rejected in SmartRecruiters for reasons that do not automatically re-trigger the native re-approval flow, the Approvals API provides a clean programmatic path to restart the process. The end-to-end integration pattern is:

  1. Subscribe to the job.approval.step.rejected webhook event.
  2. Call GET /jobs/{jobId}/approvals/latest to retrieve the approvalRequestId.
  3. Optionally call GET /approvals-api/v201910/approvals/{approvalId}/comments to capture the rejection reason.
  4. After the recruiter makes the necessary updates, call POST /approvals-api/v201910/approvals with baseId set to the original approval ID to create a fresh approval chain.

 

This approach gives integration teams full control over the re-approval lifecycle, ensures no job falls through the cracks after a rejection, and provides a complete audit trail of rejection reasons and re-submission history.

Thanks

Kunal

entry.title: Re: IAS Integration Issue: EC to ECP User Replication – U...
entry.content:
Dear customer,

ECP is built on SAP ABAP, where user names (BNAME field in SU01/USR02) are hard-limited to 12 characters — this is a platform constraint that cannot be extended. IPS maps the IAS username directly to this ABAP field, so any username exceeding 12 characters causes replication to fail.

Option 1 — Enable Internal Numbering in ECP (Recommended)

Configure ECP to ignore the IPS-supplied username and generate its own short internal ID instead (format: SCUS + 8-digit counter, e.g. SCUS00000042). This is always within 12 characters and guaranteed unique.

  • Steps on the ECP system:
    1. Run transaction HRSFEC_ECP_CONFIG.
    2. Create a new entry:
      Context: IPS
      Scenario: USER_CREATION_RULE
      Value: INTERNAL
    3. Save. (No transport needed — this is a client-dependent customising table.)
  • On the next IPS run, new users get a generated SCUS name. Users already in a broken state in ECP should be deleted first so IPS can recreate them cleanly.
  • Documentation Configuring Mapping in Employee Central Payroll explains this configuration.

Option 2 — Map a Short, Unique Field in the IPS Transformation

If the ECP username must remain meaningful (not auto-generated), configure the IPS transformation to use a short, stable, unique field (e.g. employee number / personnel number) as the source for $.userName on the ECP target instead of the EC login name.

  • Go to IPS admin console → ECP target system → Transformations tab.
  • Update the sourcePath for $.userName to a field such as $.employeeNumber.
  • Run a test provisioning job for one affected user to validate.
  • Prerequisite: The chosen field must be unique across all users and must not change over time.

⚠️ Disclaimer: Modifying IPS transformation scripts goes beyond the scope of SAP Support. The standard transformations are provided as-is per the official SAP documentation. Any customisation — including changes to attribute mappings — is the customer's responsibility. SAP Support can guide you on the documented transformation capabilities, but cannot implement, validate, or take ownership of custom transformation logic applied to your system.

For reference, a similar field length limitation in IPS transformations has been addressed by the IPS team in KBA 3560650 - How to limit length of field in IPS transformation to avoid error caused by the field is too long.

Best regards,
SAP Support

entry.title: Your Approved Process Is Already in SharePoint. You Just Haven't Set It Up Yet.
entry.content:
Every SPG approval workflow ends the same way. The case closes, the approver receives a notification, and then someone opens SharePoint, navigates to the correct folder, downloads the BPMN from Process Manager, renames it to whatever the naming convention says, and uploads it. If they remember. If they have access. If the naming convention is still what they think it is.

The assumption baked into this step is that publishing a process to SharePoint is a separate task from approving it. Two systems, two workflows, one person bridging them manually. For teams running SPG approvals at any volume, this adds up quickly and fails silently: the approved version isn't in SharePoint, nobody notices until someone shares the wrong file, and there is no record of when the published copy was last updated.

SPG has a SharePoint Upload action. It takes about fifteen minutes to configure, requires no code, and runs at workflow close as part of the same sequence that sends the approval notification. Most teams running SPG don't know it exists.

What it actually does

The SharePoint Upload action is a service task you add to your workflow. At the point in the flow where you want the upload to happen, usually right after the approval gateway, SPG pushes a file to a SharePoint location you specify in the action configuration. The file can be a static attachment, a workflow variable, or a BPMN export generated earlier in the same workflow.

That last option is the useful combination. Pair it with the BPMN Export as XML action earlier in the flow, and the full sequence becomes: process approved, BPMN exported, file uploaded to SharePoint, approval notification sent. No manual steps. No separate system to check.

Approval task (human review)
→ Gateway: Approved / Rejected
→ BPMN Export as XML (generates file, stores in variable)
→ SharePoint Upload (pushes file to target folder)
→ Notify approver and requestor
→ End

The complete workflow: approval gateway routes to BPMN export and SharePoint upload on approval, or directly to rejection notification

Adding the BPMN export

To upload the current version of the process rather than a manually attached file, add a BPMN Export as XML action before the SharePoint Upload step. Configure it to write the export into a workflow variable. That variable is what the SharePoint Upload action reads from.

BPMN Export as XML is a separate action available under the same service task list. It exports the model associated with the case at the time the action runs. If your workflow is triggered by an approval workflow, the revision ID flows in automatically. If it's triggered manually or by form submission, you'll need a revision ID variable in scope.

Configuring the SharePoint Upload action

Prerequisites: an organization administrator must enable the SharePoint File Upload action under Organization Settings → Actions, configure a connection (SharePoint tenant, site, credentials, drive, base path), and toggle it on for modelers. This is done once per workspace configuration.

In the workflow editor, add a Service Task after the BPMN Export step, select SharePoint File Upload from the External Actions list, and choose a configuration. Under the Inputs tab, set:

   
Input  What to set
Target folderThe destination folder within the configured SharePoint drive
Upload file(s)Select the workflow variable holding the BPMN export

SharePoint Upload configuration: target folder selected from the site tree, XML File variable wired as the upload source

Full reference: External Actions - SharePoint File Upload on SAP Help Portal. Admin setup: Enabling SharePoint File Upload as an Organization Administrator.

Download this workflow template (attached), rename it to .bpmn , replace YOUR_BPMN_EXPORT_CONFIGURATION_ID and YOUR_SHAREPOINT_CONFIGURATION_ID with your workspace values, then import into SPG.

What this replaces

The manual step it removes is small enough that most teams don't consider it a problem worth solving. But small, inconsistent steps have a way of adding up. SharePoint ends up with a mix of approved and draft versions, uploaded at different times and named differently depending on who uploaded them. The most recently approved process may or may not be the most recent file in the folder.

When the upload is part of the workflow, the SharePoint folder becomes a reliable output of the governance process rather than a manual filing task. The approved version is always there, always current, always named consistently. For teams that use SharePoint as the distribution layer for their process documentation, this is a meaningful change that takes 15 minutes of configuration.

Part of the SPG Hidden Gems series: short posts on features, patterns, and fixes that rarely make it into the main documentation but save real time once you know them. Questions or feedback? Reach out to sap-spg-pms@sap.com.

entry.title: Re: Send Material Reserved Stock to Sales Force via API o...
entry.content:
Hi,

The Material Stock API won't give it to you, because a reservation is not a stock type. The reserved quantity lives in the reservation items, and there is a released API for them: API_RESERVATION_DOCUMENT_SRV (OData V2, entity A_ReservationDocumentItem), plus a V4 version, API_RESERVATION_DOCUMENT. Under both is the CDS view I_ReservationDocumentItem, which is released for key user apps and for ABAP Cloud in my S/4HANA 2023 lab. Your tags say Public Cloud, and the SAP Business Accelerator Hub lists API_RESERVATION_DOCUMENT_SRV and the A2X V4 version in the S/4HANA Cloud Public Edition package, so you should find it there as a communication scenario.

The open reserved quantity per item is ResvnItmRequiredQtyInBaseUnit minus ResvnItmWithdrawnQtyInBaseUnit, and only for open goods issue items:

  • DebitCreditCode = 'H' (issue, 'S' would be a planned receipt)
  • ReservationItemIsFinallyIssued = false
  • ReservationItmIsMarkedForDeltn = false

The entity of the API has the same field names, so you have two ways. Call the API with $filter on Product, Plant and the three conditions and sum per material in Salesforce or in the middleware. Or, if you want SAP to send one number per material, build a small custom CDS view with the SUM on top of I_ReservationDocumentItem and expose it as your own OData service (in Public Cloud that is developer extensibility, with ABAP Cloud). The same logic as ABAP SQL, which ran in my lab:

SELECT Product, Plant,
       SUM( ResvnItmRequiredQtyInBaseUnit - ResvnItmWithdrawnQtyInBaseUnit ) AS OpenReservedQty
  FROM I_ReservationDocumentItem
  WHERE DebitCreditCode                = 'H'
    AND ReservationItemIsFinallyIssued = @abap_false
    AND ReservationItmIsMarkedForDeltn = @abap_false
  GROUP BY Product, Plant
  INTO TABLE @DATA(lt_reserved).

It returned 13 material and plant combinations. Without the deletion flag it returned 19, and one material went from 2,516 to 2,542, so don't skip that condition.

One thing to agree with the business first: sales order requirements are not reservations. In my lab they are in a different table (VBBE), so if "reserved" for your users also means quantities promised to customers, this view won't show them.

What I didn't test: calling the OData service from outside SAP, and Public Cloud itself. For Public Cloud I only checked the API catalog, so confirm the communication scenario name in your system.

entry.content:
What used to take more than eight hours now takes 13 minutes. With 2608 Release upgrade, SAP S/4HANA Public Cloud now completes production system upgrades in an average of 13 minutes, a 97% reduction from more than eight hours in 2019, validated consistently across more than 2,780 production systems worldwide. Non-production systems perform even better, averaging 7 minutes, bringing the overall landscape average to 10 minutes. This is not a theoretical benchmark. It is the measured, repeatable outcome of seven years of sustained engineering commitment.

The numbers tell the story clearly:

YearAverage Production DowntimeKey Driver
2019516 minutes (approximately 8.6 hours)Legacy in-place upgrade model
2021144 minutesIntroduction of Blue-Green architecture
2023Temporary increase35% expansion in customer base
202441 minutesContinuous optimization
202519 minutesParallel preparation maturity
202613 minutesCurrent benchmark


The breakthrough stems from a fundamental rethinking of how upgrades are delivered. Rather than taking a live system offline, SAP uses Blue Green deployment architecture, building an entirely new upgraded environment in parallel while customers continue working.
By the time the switchover begins, software installation, database schema updates, customization validation, and integration testing are already complete. The 13-minute window covers only the final data synchronization, traffic switchover, and application server restart.

Because 96% of upgrade work happens during the parallel preparation phase, customer-specific factors such as data volume, custom code complexity, and integration landscape do not extend downtime. Whether a customer has 100 GB or 10 TB of data, the switchover remains consistently brief. The complexity is handled during uptime, not during the maintenance window.

For businesses, this change is material. Manufacturing customers no longer require extended production shutdowns. Financial institutions maintain service level agreement uptime and minimize regulatory exposure. Global enterprises find coordination across time zones dramatically simpler. The predictability of 13-minute upgrades also makes the half yearly release cadence of SAP S/4HANA Public Cloud operationally viable, allowing customers to stay current with the latest innovations without disrupting Operations.

One distinction is worth noting when evaluating vendors. SAP reports actual measured downtime, defined as the time from when the last user transaction completes to when the first user can log back in, averaged across all production systems. This differs from scheduled maintenance windows, which represent calendar time that is blocked but may not reflect true system unavailability. Customers should ask whether a vendor's published figures represent reserved windows or actual downtime.

The shift from more than eight hours to 13 minutes is not simply an operational improvement. It is a change in what customers should expect from enterprise cloud enterprise resource planning. With a clear roadmap targeting fewer than five minutes and a longer-term vision of eliminating scheduled maintenance entirely.

SAP S/4HANA Public Cloud is setting a new standard. The question for customers is no longer how long upgrades will take, but when they will become completely invisible.

entry.title: 292 S/4HANA tables answer one thing to ABAP and another to the database. I counted them
entry.content:
Ask an S/4HANA 2023 system how much unrestricted stock is in table MARD. With ABAP SQL, my lab says 4,860,442. With native SQL on HANA, same table, same client: 3,500.

Same system, same second. Only one of the two answers is right.

Ok, but what does this change in my day? If you write AMDP, native SQL, HANA views on the ABAP schema, or if you are connecting an AI agent straight to the database, quite a lot. So I went to my labs and counted.

Where the difference comes from

In S/4HANA many classic tables have a replacement object: a CDS view registered in DD02L, field VIEWREF. When ABAP SQL reads the table, the database interface reads the CDS view instead. MARD is redirected to NSDM_V_MARD, which calculates the stock from MATDOC. The physical MARD still has its 937 rows with the right keys, but nobody maintains the stock columns anymore.

The ABAP documentation (chapter "DDIC - Replacement Objects") lists who is NOT redirected: native SQL (ADBC, EXEC SQL), AMDP, database procedures and views, and the one I didn't expect: ABAP SQL on a CDS view that selects from such a table. In the words of the documentation, "The replacement object must be accessed directly."

SAP has its own example of that last case. FAA_ANEK_ORI is a CDS view whose whole definition is select * from anek. ABAP SQL on ANEK returns 20 rows in my 2023 lab and 197 in my 2020 lab. ABAP SQL on FAA_ANEK_ORI returns 0 in both.

How many tables are like this

One SELECT on DD02L gives the list. S/4HANA 2023 (release 758) has 292 of them, S/4HANA 2020 (release 755) has 293. 179 are transparent tables and 113 are DDIC database views. Between the two releases only 2 entered (/SCMB/GTS_MOT and /SCMB/GTS_MOTT) and 3 left, so the list is stable enough to keep in mind.

Most of them are the ones you know from the simplification list: inventory (MSEG, MKPF, MARD, MCHB, MSKA, MSLB and their history tables), material valuation (MBEW, EBEW, QBEW, OBEW), asset accounting (ANEA, ANEK, ANEP, ANLC, ANLP), CO line items (COEP) and the old ledger tables like FAGLFLEXA.

What surprised me most was the delivery class. 47 of the 292 are customizing tables. T012K, the house bank accounts, is one of them: ABAP SQL returns 10 rows in my 2023 lab, native SQL returns 198. Its replacement, V_T012K_BAM, reads FCLM_BAM_T012K_BASE from Bank Account Management, and the source has this comment from SAP: "Redirection interface for T012k. Re-generating from template required. NEVER RELEASE!!!". The EWM handling unit types in /SCWM/THUTYP are another one, with 26 rows through ABAP and 0 in the database.

The numbers

Each table counted twice in each lab, ABAP SQL first and native SQL on HANA second, always for the logon client.

TableS/4HANA 2023, ABAP / nativeS/4HANA 2020, ABAP / native
MSEG, rows1,440 / 18,394 / 0
MKPF, rows1,020 / 13,780 / 0
MARD, rows937 / 9371,064 / 1,064
MARD, sum of LABST4,860,442 / 3,500501,385,358.803 / 3,875
MBEW, sum of LBKUM4,865,306 / 0501,388,829.803 / 0
ANEK, rows20 / 0197 / 0
ANEP, rows40 / 0679 / 0
ANLC, rows68 / 01,076 / 0
COEP, rows816 / 212,995 / 32
BSIM, rows780 / 07,872 / 0
T012K, rows10 / 19816 / 61
/SCWM/THUTYP, rows26 / 07 / 2
MATDOC, rows (no replacement object)1,460 / 1,4608,397 / 8,397

Two lines in this table matter more than the big differences. MATDOC is the control: no replacement object, same count both ways. And MARD and MBEW have exactly the same number of rows both ways. If your test is "count the rows and compare", everything looks fine, and the stock is still wrong.

What I take from this

Inside ABAP, read these tables with ABAP SQL directly, not through a CDS view of your own that selects from them, and not in AMDP. If you need the data in CDS or AMDP, read the replacement object, or better a released CDS view. For stock, I_MaterialStock_2 is released in my 2023 lab.

Outside ABAP the rule is simpler: anything that reads the database directly gets the old table, and nothing warns it. That includes the AI agents many of us are building now. If your agent can run SQL on the S/4HANA schema, this list belongs in its instructions, or better, the agent should ask the application layer and not the database.

To see the list in your own system:

SELECT tabname, viewref, contflag
  FROM dd02l
  WHERE as4local = 'A'
    AND viewref  <> ' '
  INTO TABLE @DATA(lt_redirected).

All the numbers come from my S/4HANA 2020 and 2023 lab systems, so the data is demo data and your counts will be different. I didn't run an AMDP for this post: that part comes from the ABAP documentation. I also didn't check S/4HANA 2025 or the Cloud editions.

Which of these tables does your HANA-side code, or your agent, read directly today? I'd really like to know which one surprised you, so feel free to comment.

entry.title: Re: How abap2UI5 Complements RAP and Fiori Elements – Now Also as a Custom Control
entry.content:
Hi @Gayathri_S ,

thanks a lot! Honestly, for really complex UI requirements a UI5 freestyle app in JavaScript gives you the most freedom. Especially when the logic has to live in the browser, like offline support, heavy client-side interaction or a lot of device features, freestyle is the right choice.

In practice, though, the deciding factor is often not the UI but the team. Most SAP projects I see are staffed by ABAP teams who know ABAP, ATC, transports and the business data very well, and much less JavaScript, npm and the UI5 tooling. For them abap2UI5 is a great fit: they can learn it quickly and build powerful apps in the language and tools they already use. And they don’t have to maintain a second technology stack afterwards.

So the factors I would look at:

  • Where must the logic run? In the browser (offline, very rich interaction) → freestyle. On the server (business logic, data, authorizations) → abap2UI5 works well.
  • Who builds and maintains it? A JavaScript/UI5 team → freestyle. An ABAP team → abap2UI5.
  • Lifecycle: one ABAP class, transported like any other development, versus a separate frontend project with its own build and deployment.

Drawing a hard line is difficult. It depends more on the people and their experience than on the requirement itself. And it doesn’t have to be either-or: with the new custom control, a freestyle app can take over single screens or areas written in ABAP.

Best regards

entry.title: Simplified setup of Custom Document Grounding for SAP Joule for Consultants using CIAS Automation
entry.content:
This blog is co-authored by colleagues from SAP AI Factory @Samir_Rai, @Ananny_Tripathi . We have received considerable support from @HartmutStraub from AI RIG, @AnaghaDAnanth, @karthikeyan Mohanachandran and @ Rahul Jain from SAP CLE and @YihsuanLin from SAP J4C product management team.

1. Introduction

SAP Joule for Consultants is a generative AI copilot built specifically for the SAP consulting community. Grounded in over 9 terabytes of curated SAP knowledge — including 18+ million pages of SAP documentation, 100+ SAP certifications, and implementation guides — it delivers expert-level answers based on trusted SAP content.

But every consulting organization carries its own body of knowledge: internal delivery frameworks, proprietary accelerators, client-specific runbooks, architecture decisions, and hard-won lessons that simply don't exist in SAP's public content. Custom knowledge grounding is what bridges that gap — allowing you to connect Joule to your organization's curated content so it can answer not just as an SAP expert, but as your team's expert.

What Custom Knowledge Grounding Does

Custom Knowledge Grounding extends SAP Joule for Consultants with your organization’s own documents. The documents are uploaded to a data repository, indexed by SAP AI Core Document Grounding, and retrieved at runtime to ground SAP Joule for Consultants’ answers. Users get responses that combine the SAP-curated content SAP Joule for Consultants ships with and their firm’s own methodologies, policies, and delivery standards.

Configuring custom knowledge grounding manually, however, involves its own set of connected steps — setting up the right services, connecting knowledge sources, configuring trust and authorization, and ensuring everything is wired together correctly in the right sequence. Done manually, this takes considerable time and leaves room for misses and misconfiguration.

Cloud Integration Automation Service (CIAS) changes that. In this blog, we walk through how to use CIAS to automate the setup of custom knowledge grounding for SAP Joule for Consultants — end to end, in the correct order, with a guided workflow that replaces the manual overhead with a reliable, repeatable process.

2. The Role of CIAS Automation

Cloud Integration Automation service provides you a guided workflow to activate SAP cloud solutions. The guided workflow contains instructions for manual and automated tasks to enable an easy and quick integration configuration setup. The service is also used to integrate SAP Cloud solutions to on-premises solutions or other cloud solutions. It’s a free service available for the customers.

For SAP Joule for Consultants, CIAS plays a key role in simplifying activation. Instead of working across multiple tools separately — SAP BTP Cockpit, SAP Cloud Identity, SAP Central Business Configuration, and SAP for Me — and having to get the sequence right yourself, CIAS provides one guided workflow that handles these tasks end-to-end, in the correct order.

Here’s the advantage it brings compared to the manual activation:

  2. Copy the JSON.

     

  3. Go back to SAP Joule for consultant console and select Custom knowledge Grounding -> Sources & Pipelines-> and click on connect

     

  4. Select the JSON format and paste the Destination service JSON that you copied from the SAP Joule for consultants subaccount and then click on next.

     

  5. Select the sources and then click on Save.
  6. Select the complete task from the CIAS automation tool  and then click on finish to complete the automation workflow.

     

     

    Congratulations! Custom knowledge grounding is enabled in SAP Joule for Consultants.

Manage Sources & Pipelines

    • Monitor document grounding sources and pipelines, review pipeline status and processing information, and manage source configuration and access control.

      Sources & Pipelines

    For more information, see Managing Access Control for Custom Knowledge Grounding on the SAP Help Portal.

    Understand Pipeline Status

  1. For details, check the documents in Bruno or in the SAP AI Launchpad. For support, open a ticket under component CA-ML-RAGE . Troubleshooting the AI Core Document Grounding pipeline is out of scope for SAP Joule for Consultants.

     Refresh the Pipeline View and Re-Index Data
