entry.title: Re: How to determine T052-ZTAGG for BSIK/BSAK documents w...
entry.content:
Hi  @RitaZ-12345 ,

In such cases I like to search for some standard object which is performing calculation I'm looking for.

For your case, I found an example in FM FI_TERMS_OF_PAYMENT_PROPOSE:

  IF  NOT E_ZFBDT    IS INITIAL
  AND     T052-ZTAGG GT   0.
    SELECT * FROM  T052
             WHERE ZTERM EQ I_ZTERM
             AND   ZTAGG GE E_ZFBDT+6(2)
             ORDER BY PRIMARY KEY.
      EXIT.
    ENDSELECT.

This means that, if the payment terms have limit days customized (T052-ZTAGG GT 0), the system is selecting all the records with Day Limit (ZTAGG - Day of the month until which the corresponding terms are valid) higher or equal to base line date day of the month. Then, by ordering by primary key, system ensures the first entry, with lowest day limit (ZTAGG), is considered for determining the rest of the payment terms conditions.

This is just confirming what @RaymondGiuseppi had said, but with other words 🙂

I hope this helps.

BR,

Filipe

entry.title: Re: Own Application Log App
entry.content:
Hi,

I can't look into your BTP system, but I checked the release state of the application log API in an S/4HANA 2023 system. What is released for ABAP Cloud there is the read side of the API: CL_BALI_LOG_DB (LOAD_LOG, LOAD_LOGS_VIA_FILTER), CL_BALI_LOG_FILTER and the getter interfaces IF_BALI_HEADER_GETTER and IF_BALI_ITEM_GETTER. A package with ABAP for Cloud Development can only use released objects, which is what your deployment error is saying about the service you reused.

The way that stays inside the rules is a small service of your own on top of that API:

  1. A custom entity (DEFINE CUSTOM ENTITY with @ObjectModel.query.implementedBy) for the log headers, and a second one for the items if you want to drill down.
  2. A query provider class (IF_RAP_QUERY_PROVIDER) that reads through CL_BALI_LOG_DB.
  3. Service definition, an OData V4 UI binding and a Fiori elements list report on top.

The core of the query provider, reading the headers of your object:

DATA(lo_filter) = cl_bali_log_filter=>create( )->set_descriptor( object = '/NS/EXPORT' ).
DATA(lt_logs) = cl_bali_log_db=>get_instance( )->load_logs_via_filter(
                  filter           = lo_filter
                  read_only_header = abap_true ).
LOOP AT lt_logs INTO DATA(lo_log).
  DATA(lo_header) = lo_log->get_header( ).
  APPEND VALUE #( loghandle    = lo_log->get_handle( )
                  externalid   = lo_header->external_id
                  logtimestamp = lo_header->log_timestamp
                  loguser      = lo_header->log_user
                  errors       = lo_header->number_error_items ) TO lt_result.
ENDLOOP.

Around it you need the usual parts of a query provider: catch CX_BALI_RUNTIME, set the total count when io_request asks for it, and apply the paging from io_request->get_paging( ) before set_data. For the items, LOAD_LOG with the handle, then GET_ALL_ITEMS and GET_MESSAGE_TEXT on each item. If you have many logs, pass the user's filter into SET_TIME_INTERVAL and SET_MAXIMUM_LOG_NUMBER of the filter object instead of loading everything and paging in memory.

What I checked: a local class with this select method compiles in S/4HANA 2023 (syntax check only, nothing saved), and the same code with a wrong header attribute fails. I didn't build the custom entity or the app, and I didn't test it on BTP ABAP Environment, where the release state is what counts.

entry.title: Re: ME23N needs to display the IR Reference field
entry.content: @EOB good find from your developer, OUTTAB_CHANGE of ME_POHIST_DISP_CUST is the right place. I looked at the interface in an S/4HANA 2023 system and would add three things before it goes live. First, CT_OUTTAB is a generic STANDARD TABLE and IM_POHIST_BADI_CALLER says which history view is calling (the interface has 10 caller constants, from C_CALLER_STANDARD to C_CALLER_ZEIT), so the same code runs for all of them: check the caller, and check that each ASSIGN COMPONENT worked (IS ASSIGNED) before using the field symbol, otherwise a view without BELNR, GJAHR or XBLNR ends in a runtime error. Second, only change invoice lines: on goods receipt lines BELNR is a material document number and the code still looks it up in RBKP. In my two labs no goods receipt number matched an invoice number (0 of 687 and 0 of 2,507 lines), because the number ranges are different, but nothing in the code guarantees that. Third, SELECT SINGLE * inside the loop reads the whole RBKP row for every line, so read only XBLNR, or collect BELNR and GJAHR first and read them in one SELECT. entry.title: UAE eInvoice: Capturing Down Payments and Prepaid Amounts
entry.content:
Overview

Down payments are common in many industries. When a customer pays a deposit upfront and then receives an invoice for the remaining balance, the UAE PINT AE eInvoice standard requires the invoice to explicitly declare the amount already paid. This is the prepaid amount field.

This post walks through the three main SAP process paths for handling down payments and explains how the prepaid amount gets captured in the XML eInvoice for each one.

The Prepaid Amount in PINT AE

In the PINT AE (Peppol International Invoice) standard adopted by the UAE, the monetary totals section of an invoice carries:

Term ID Name XML Element

IBT-112Invoice total amount with VATcbc:TaxInclusiveAmount
IBT-113Paid amountcbc:PrepaidAmount
IBT-115Amount due for paymentcbc:PayableAmount

The relationship is straightforward:

PayableAmount (IBT-115) = TaxInclusiveAmount (IBT-112) − PrepaidAmount (IBT-113)

A down payment invoice (the first document) carries the full down payment amount as its TaxInclusiveAmount with PayableAmount equal to that same amount and PrepaidAmount of zero.

The invoice references the down payment and sets PrepaidAmount equal to the down payment amount already collected, so PayableAmount reflects only the remaining balance due.

<!-- Invoice monetary totals example -->
<cac:LegalMonetaryTotal>
  <cbc:LineExtensionAmount currencyID="AED">10000.00</cbc:LineExtensionAmount>
  <cbc:TaxExclusiveAmount currencyID="AED">10000.00</cbc:TaxExclusiveAmount>
  <cbc:TaxInclusiveAmount currencyID="AED">10500.00</cbc:TaxInclusiveAmount>
  <cbc:PrepaidAmount currencyID="AED">2100.00</cbc:PrepaidAmount>
  <cbc:PayableAmount currencyID="AED">8400.00</cbc:PayableAmount>
</cac:LegalMonetaryTotal>

Scenario 1: SD Down Payment via Billing Plan

This is the fully integrated SD path. Down payments are modelled as a billing plan on the sales order, and every invoice — both the down payment request and the final delivery-based invoice — is created as a standard SD billing document.

Process Flow

VA01 | Manage Sales Orders (F1873)
Create Sales Order with Billing Plan (including Down Payment milestone)VA01 | Manage Sales Orders (F1873)
Create Down Payment Request (DP Request refers to SO and the DP Billing Plan)
VA02 | Manage Sales Orders (F1873)
Remove Billing Block on the DP Request
VF01 | Create Billing Documents (F0798)
Create Down Payment Billing Document → eDocument created (Down Payment Invoice)
VL01N | Manage Outbound Deliveries (F0867A) 
Create Outbound Delivery
VF01 | Create Billing Documents (F0798)
Create Billing Document (refers to Outbound Delivery) → eDocument created (prepaid amount captured)

How the Prepaid Amount Is Captured

When the final billing document is created in VF01 against the outbound delivery, SAP SD billing knows about the prior down payment billing document linked to the same sales order via the billing plan. The billing value calculation nets out the already-invoiced down payment amount.

The eDocument mapping reads the billing document's financial data — specifically the cleared down payment offset — and places this value into cbc:PrepaidAmount. The down payment billing document itself becomes the Down Payment Invoice eDocument (with PrepaidAmount = 0), while the final delivery invoice carries PrepaidAmount equal to the down payment value.

Key Points

  • The down payment billing document is submitted as a separate eDocument before the final invoice.
  • No FI posting is needed to trigger the prepaid amount: the entire lifecycle stays within SD billing.
  • The billing plan configuration (payment milestone type, percentages or fixed amounts) drives the down payment value.

Scenario 2: SD-FI Down Payment

In this scenario the sales order exists in SD, but the down payment is posted through the FI module directly rather than through a SD billing document. This is common when the down payment is handled by the finance department independently from the SD billing cycle.

Process Flow

VA01 | Manage Sales Orders (F1873)
Create Sales Order
F-37 | Post Down Payment Request – Customers (F1689)
Create Down Payment Request (optional; creates a noted item)
F-29 | Post Down Payment – Customers
Create Down Payment Document (optional, refers to DP Request) → eDocument created (Down Payment Invoice)
VL01N | Manage Outbound Deliveries (F0867A) 
Create Outbound Delivery
VF01 | Create Billing Documents (F0798) 
Create Billing Document (refers to Outbound Delivery) → eDocument created (should NOT be submitted yet)
F-39 | Clear Incoming Down Payments – Customers (F8969)
Clear Down Payment against the final customer invoice → eDocument updated with prepaid amount

How the Prepaid Amount Is Captured

The VF01 billing document triggers the initial creation of the eDocument, but at that moment the down payment has not yet been applied against the open receivable. The eDocument is therefore held — it should not be submitted to the tax authority at this point.

The clearing step (F-39) links the down payment posting to the open invoice item. After clearing, the eDocument framework detects the change on the underlying accounting document and updates the eDocument. The cleared down payment amount flows into cbc:PrepaidAmount, and cbc:PayableAmount is recalculated as the net amount due.

Only after F-39 is the eDocument ready for submission.

Key Points

  • The Down Payment Document from F-29 generates its own eDocument — the Down Payment Invoice submitted before the final invoice.
  • The final billing document eDocument must not be submitted before the F-39 clearing step.
  • F-39 triggers the eDocument update that populates PrepaidAmount.
  • F-37 (the DP Request) is a noted item and does not generate an eDocument on its own.

Scenario 3: FI Down Payment (No SD Sales Order)

This scenario applies to standalone financial transactions — service invoices, lease prepayments, or any situation where no SD sales order is involved. The entire lifecycle runs through FI.

Process Flow

F-37 | Post Down Payment Request – Customers (F1689)
Create Down Payment Request (optional; creates a noted item)
F-29 | Post Down Payment – Customers
Create Down Payment Document (optional, refers to DP Request) → eDocument created (Down Payment Invoice)
FB70 | Create Outgoing Invoices
Create Customer Invoice → eDocument created (should NOT be submitted yet)
F-39 | Clear Incoming Down Payments – Customers  (F8969)
Clear Down Payment against the customer invoice → eDocument updated with prepaid amount

How the Prepaid Amount Is Captured

The mechanism mirrors Scenario 2. FB70 posts the customer invoice and the eDocument framework creates an eDocument, but the document must not be submitted before clearing.

F-39 applies the previously posted down payment against the open invoice item. The eDocument is updated with the cleared amount as PrepaidAmount. The net PayableAmount reflects only the residual balance owed by the customer.

Key Points

  • F-37 creates a noted item only — no FI document, no eDocument.
  • F-29 generates the actual down payment posting and the corresponding Down Payment Invoice eDocument.
  • FB70 triggers initial eDocument creation, but submission waits for F-39.
  • F-39 is the event that finalises the PrepaidAmount on the final invoice eDocument.

Summary Comparison

 Scenario 1 (SD Billing Plan) Scenario 2 (SD-FI)Scenario 3 (FI Only)
Down Payment InvoiceVF01 billing documentF-29 postingF-29 posting
Final InvoiceVF01 billing documentVF01 billing documentFB70 posting
Prepaid Amount SourceSD billing plan nettingF-39 clearingF-39 clearing
eDocument hold required?NoYes (before F-39)Yes (before F-39)
Clearing step needed?NoF-39F-39

Submission Sequence

Regardless of scenario, the submission sequence to the UAE tax authority must always be:

  1. Down Payment Invoice eDocument — submitted first, confirms the advance payment collected.
  2. Invoice eDocument — submitted after the prepaid amount is resolved, carries PrepaidAmount and reduced PayableAmount.

Submitting the final invoice before the down payment invoice, or submitting the final invoice before the clearing step in Scenarios 2 and 3, will result in an invalid eDocument with a missing

or incorrect PrepaidAmount.

Fiori App Reference

Transaction Fiori App Name App IDVA01 Manage Sales Orders F1873VA02 Manage Sales Orders F1873VF01 Create Billing Documents F0798VL01N Manage Outbound Deliveries F0867AF-37 Post Down Payment Request – Customers F1689F-29 Post Down Payment – Customers  F-39 Clear Incoming Down Payments – Customers F8969FB70 Create Outgoing Invoices  

Confirm via the SAP Fiori Apps Reference Library.

Configuration Note

For the eDocument framework to correctly identify a billing document or FI posting as a down payment and map it to the appropriate PINT AE document type, the DRC process configuration for UAE must be active and the down payment process subtype must be correctly assigned. Verify this in the DRC Cockpit under the UAE country scope.

FI Document Type for Down Payments (Scenarios 2 and 3)

The FI document type assigned to down payment postings (F-29) must be different from the document type used for normal customer payment receipts. The eDocument framework relies on the document type to classify an incoming posting as a down payment and trigger the Down Payment Invoice eDocument. If down payment postings and regular customer payments share the same document type, the framework cannot distinguish between them — eDocuments will be created for both, causing regular customer payment receipts to incorrectly trigger eDocument generation..

Related Resources

  • PINT AE Business Rules — docs.peppol.eu/poac/ae/
  • SAP Note 3705171 — UAE e-Invoicing Implementation Overview
  • KBA 3729281 — UAE eInvoicing Programme FAQ
  • SAP Blog — What You Need to Know on the UAE DCTCE Model and the Rollout Plan

entry.title: Joule Studio Live Demo: Building a Purchase Requisition Agent in 45 Minutes
entry.content:
In our second Hackathon Alumni session, Luca Tallarita, Senior Development Consultant at SAP, took a use case submitted by community members and built an AI agent with Joule Studio. This was live and unscripted, while around 30+ participants asked questions that many early adopters are probably wondering about right now also. The timing was actually good: as the SAP TechEd 2026 Innovation News Guide puts it, "general availability for Autonomous Enterprise assistants and agents, Joule Work and Joule Studio is now underway in a phased approach." 

Context and Community

The SAP "Business meets AI" hackathons in Zurich, Munich, Berlin and Vienna brought together business and technical users to explore AI use cases on SAP BTP. After the first alumni session, where teams shared what happened after the hackathon and their use cases (see From Prototype to Practice), the community voted for a hands-on Joule Studio session as the next topic.

Quick Pulse Check: Where Does the Community Stand?

We started with a Mentimeter poll as check-in. Nobody had "never heard of" Joule Studio. Nine had heard of it, seven had already seen demos or completed e-learnings, and three were actively using the first version. That gave Luca a solid baseline to skip the basics and go deeper. And we see that the Alumni is an informed cohort. 

Purchase Requisition Creation as Use Case

Luca and his team developed a use case submission and voting app, which is a great approach to involve people and crowdsource ideas. From three submitted use cases, Luca selected a purchase requisition scenario. The challenge here was: Procurement staff spend excessive manual effort processing purchase order confirmations received via email, leading to inefficiencies and delayed updates in SAP.

A typical process that takes significant manual effort and could benefit from AI support. 
See below the screenshot from the app and the AI enhanced description.

Joule Studio's Intent-Based Development Process

Luca then walked us through the four-step process that Joule Studio follows:

1. Intent Summary

The starting point is always a business problem described in natural language, not technical specifications. Joule Studio asks clarifying questions (e.g. "Which S/4HANA deployment does your organization use?" or "Which PR creation scenarios should the agent support?") until it has a complete picture. The more detail you provide upfront, the fewer questions it asks.

There is also a "Quick Create" option that skips the clarifying questions. Joule Studio then makes assumptions based on standard processes. This is useful for speed, but the guided path produces more tailored, concreter results.

The intent file that Joule Studio generates includes the business challenge, goals and success criteria, milestones, business architecture (mapped to SAP end-to-end processes via the EKX knowledge graph), and a fit-gap analysis of available APIs and MCP servers. Below in the screenshot you see how you can chat with the intent summary to iteratively optimate the Intent.

2. Product Requirements Document (PRD)

Based on the intent, Joule Studio generates a structured PRD covering: purpose and value proposition, expected time savings and business metrics, user profiles and personas, user goals and tasks, product principles, scope definition (in/out), and a prioritized list of requirements (must have, high want, nice to have, non-functional). It also includes a solution architecture recommendation with an overview of the architecture, integration points, etc. 

3. Specifications

The specification is the technical bridge between requirements and code. It contains step-by-step instructions for the coding agent: guidelines for the agent framework (Python), skill definitions, MCP server configurations, and dependency management. This step is primarily relevant for developers who want to review or adjust the technical approach. The good thing is, that you also can check the sources and edit them for example. 

4. Build Solution

After confirming the specification, you tell Joule Studio to build. In Luca's case, the coding phase took roughly 15 minutes. Joule Studio generates the agent code, creates MCP servers for each required API (translating SAP APIs into MCP format), writes test cases, and iterates until tests pass. 

The result is a complete asset folder with an AI agent and multiple MCP servers, ready for preview and deployment.

The Preview enables interacting with the Agent

Joule Studio includes a preview mode where you can interact with the generated agent using mock data. Luca asked the agent "What can you do for me?" and it listed three capabilities: creating a purchase requisition from a framework agreement, from a catalogue item, or as a free text order.

He then tested it with "Create a PR for a new MacBook" and the agent walked through the process, checking framework agreements and catalogue items. With real system integration, the agent would pull live data from S/4HANA and Ariba.

Deployment, Versioning and Collaboration

Additional capabilities Luca demonstrated were:

  • Deployment: One-click deployment from Joule Studio into an SAP-managed sub-account. Each MCP server and the agent are deployed separately and can be reused by other agents.
  • Git integration: Connect to GitHub, GitLab, or Bitbucket. Joule Studio pushes changes to the repository, and you can pull local changes back. You can also download asset files as a zip for offline development.
  • Versioning: Full lifecycle management with version history and the ability to roll back to earlier versions.
  • Collaboration: Add colleagues as viewers or editors to work on the same solution.
  • Monitoring: Analytics and monitoring dashboards for deployed assets.

Luca is a senior technical consultant and so to say early adopter and poweruser of Joule Studio. While he is not from product management we managed to answer most of the following questions.

FAQ: Questions from the Community around Joule Studio

The session generated many questions. Here are the answers as discussed:

Can Joule Studio connect to S/4HANA (public or private cloud)? Yes. If you have your own Joule Studio instance, it can access your systems. The demo ran on an internal staging environment without external system access, but the generated code prepares the integration. The final connection steps may need manual configuration.

Can you connect Joule Studio to GitHub? Yes. GitHub, GitLab, and Bitbucket are supported. Joule Studio pushes changes to the repository, and you can push local changes back.

Is MCP connectivity for external tools planned? MCP connectivity to SAP tools is available. Re Connectivity to external (non-SAP) MCP tools you may check the official documentation (or ask Joule for Consultants :-).

How is Joule Studio activated? Is it a BTP service? Joule Studio is entitled through the SAP for Me portal. A dedicated sub-account is created and SAP-managed. It is not activated like a regular BTP service.

What are the prerequisites? A BTP global account is the main prerequisite. LeanIX and Signavio integration is optional but obviously improves results, as Joule Studio can then scan your actual processes and system landscape.

Can you upload custom process descriptions or templates? Not as templates directly, but you can edit the generated files (intent, PRD, specifications) and paste your own content. With LeanIX and Signavio in place, your process descriptions feed into the generation automatically.

Are standard SAP processes sufficient without Signavio? Joule Studio knows standard SAP processes through the EKX knowledge graph. Without customer-specific process documentation via Signavio, it uses standard processes as the default. Results are more accurate with Signavio, but it is not required.

What is the relationship between the previous Joule Studio and the current version? They are different products. The skill creation from the previous version is now one option among many in the current Joule Studio (available under the "Extensions" tab). RE migration path you might also check the official documentation. (one thing i find also noteworthy: the previous version was not pro-code).

How are custom skills handled? Custom skills can be created in the Extensions area of Joule Studio. Of course you can build them also just via Claude for example. However if you want to build Skills in the SAP context, Joule studio has much more SAP context and thus is a much better option.

How are authorizations handled? The generated MCP servers do not include technical user configuration. Authorization management for system access is still a separate step. Governance of deployed applications is handled in the SAP-managed account.

Can I include custom OData APIs? Joule Studio knows published SAP APIs from the API Hub. For custom APIs, you need to provide the information manually in the intent or PRD. Joule Studio will include it in the build process but cannot discover custom APIs automatically.

Can the agent be integrated into other AI chatbots like Copilot? The agent is A2A (agent-to-agent) enabled and accessible via an endpoint URL. It can communicate with other agents that support the A2A protocol. The specific integration steps depend on the target environment.

How does deployment work? What about integration with SAP Work Zone? After deployment, the agent is available behind an endpoint URL. It can be integrated into Joule Work or other agent landscapes via A2A. The specific Work Zone integration path was not demonstrated in this session.

What about pricing and early adopter care? For early adopter questions, contact your dedicated program manager through the Early Adopter Care program. For pricing, please contact your sales contacts at SAP.

Reflections: 400 Use Cases and Counting

Sascha Faller highlighted the team behind Joule Studio: young, engaged developers who consistently demonstrate the tool live at events, under pressure, with real customer use cases. Luca shared that his team has been at 34 events so far, with 24 more planned, and has built 400 use cases with Joule Studio. As Luca put it: "When we started in May, we ourselves saw progress and improvements in the tool really rapidly. I think now we're at a stage where it's really fast, it really gets great results."

Luca's personal reflection on the tool's value: developers already have the technical skills to automate repetitive work, but business users often lack the technical capability to do so. Joule Studio bridges that gap. A business user can describe a challenge, and Joule Studio builds a working prototype. This also improves collaboration between business and technical teams: the business describes the problem, Joule Studio creates a prototype, and the technical team understands exactly what needs to be built.

In his experience, the learning curve is steep. First-timers can create agents with it, and the process itself is straightforward once you understand the chat-based interaction pattern.

Community Feedback: The Word Cloud

The closing Mentimeter asked participants to describe their impression of Joule Studio in one word. From 10 responses: exciting (2x), promising, collaborative, the future, fast, efficient, guiding, wow, and "not so easy as it looks." A mix of optimism and realism that reflects well where the product and the market stands as it enters the phased general availability. 

What Comes Next

  • Next alumni session: Planned for January 2027. We have already one volunteer to share their teams experiences with AI. We will also try to get some experiences from the AI Agent Hackathons in November & December. If you want to present your AI journey or current challenges, please reach out.
  • More hackathons: Additional SAP "Business meets AI" hackathons are planned for the coming months.

entry.title: What's New in SAP S/4HANA Cloud Public Edition 2608.3: Two Manufacturing Innovations Worth Knowing
entry.content:
The latest feature delivery collection for SAP S/4HANA Cloud Public Edition - release 2608.3 (HFC6) - brings targeted but meaningful enhancements to manufacturing operations. While not a major release, these two updates address real day-to-day pain points for production planners and shop floor teams. Here is a closer look at what has changed and why it matters.

Controlled Routing Changes Are Now a Reality

 
For anyone working with discrete manufacturing, routing accuracy is non-negotiable. A routing defines how a product is made - the sequence of operations, work centers, and processing times. Until now, making changes to an existing routing in the Manage Routings app lacked the governance layer that many regulated and quality-conscious industries demand.
With this update, that gap is closed. When you select Edit with Change Number from the Change dropdown in the Manage Routings app, you are prompted to enter a change number before the Change Routing app even opens.
 
Manage Routings - Edit with Change Number
 
Every modification made in that session is then recorded under that change number, creating a clear, auditable trail of who changed what and when.

 

This is more than a convenience feature. For industries where engineering change management is a compliance requirement - think automotive, aerospace, pharmaceuticals - having routing changes tied to a formal change number is the difference between a controlled process and an uncontrolled one. It also makes it far easier to trace back the origin of a production issue if a routing was recently modified.
 
The feature is part of scope item BJ5 (Make-to-Stock Production for Discrete Manufacturing) and requires the Manage Routings app (F5425) to be assigned to the relevant business users.

Manufacturing Order Printing Gets the Flexibility It Always Needed

 
The second enhancement tackles a limitation that has challenged manufacturing teams for a long time: the rigid, one-size-fits-all approach to printing documents for manufacturing orders.
 
Previously, when a manufacturing order was released, its documents printed automatically. Full stop. That default behavior works fine in some scenarios, but it does not reflect how many real production environments actually operate.
 
Some processes need shop floor papers at a different stage of the order lifecycle. Others should not print automatically at all - perhaps because a digital workflow handles the handover, or because unnecessary printouts are simply waste.
 
SAP has now introduced two new output modes alongside the existing default:
 
Flexible Printing of Manufacturing Orders with Output Determination

 

  • Output Control-Based: Rather than triggering automatically on release, printing is governed by your Output Determination (OPD) rules. You define the logic; the system follows it. New decision-table columns have been added for the order's output mode and eight order statuses (including Confirmed), giving you precise control over when documents are generated.
  • Manual: No automatic printing at all. Documents are printed on demand, by a user who actively requests them.
Importantly, nothing breaks on upgrade. Every existing order type retains the original Automatic on Release behavior until you explicitly change it. The new modes are configured per plant and per order type, meaning you can run different printing behaviors side by side within the same system - which is exactly what organizations with diverse production processes need.
 
To activate a new mode, navigate to your configuration environment and open either Define Order-Type-Dependent Parameters for Production Orders: 
 
Define Order-Type-Dependent Parameters for Production Orders

 

or Define Order-Type-Dependent Parameters for Process Orders: 
 
Define Order-Type-Dependent Parameters for Process Orders

 

From there, choose the Output Mode on the Implementation tab: 
 
In the Implementation Tab: Output ModeThis feature covers both discrete manufacturing (scope item BJ5) and process manufacturing based on process orders (scope item BJ8), so it is broadly applicable across production environments.

The Bigger Picture

 
Both features share a common theme: giving manufacturing teams more control and visibility. Whether that means tracing a routing change back to a specific change number, or aligning document output with the actual milestones of your production process rather than a single system event, the direction of travel is clear. SAP continues to bring the governance and flexibility that enterprise manufacturing demands into the cloud.
